title: Treasury Bills vs CDs: The Tax Break That Changes the Comparison
description: T-bill interest is exempt from state and local income tax; CD interest is not. The break-even is the bill's rate divided by one minus the state rate.
content:
Two quotes sit on the same screen: a 52-week Treasury bill and a 12-month certificate of deposit, both showing the same number. Same maturity, same headline rate, the same money going in on the same day. Nothing on either quote separates them, and that is the trap. The figure that decides the comparison is printed somewhere else — in a two-line row on a government rate table and a single sentence in an IRS publication.

Treasury states it in five words. The "Bills at a Glance" table on [TreasuryDirect](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/treasury-bills/) carries a row labeled Taxes, and the row holds two entries: "Federal tax due on interest earned" and "No state or local taxes." [Publication 550](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550) puts it in a full sentence: "Interest income from Treasury bills, notes, and bonds is subject to federal income tax but is exempt from all state and local income taxes." CD interest has no equivalent shelter. It is taxable wherever the depositor's state taxes income, on top of the federal tax both instruments owe.

What follows from that is short arithmetic. At identical headline rates, the bill's advantage over the CD equals the state marginal rate multiplied by the interest — not approximately, exactly. On $100,000 held for a year at a hypothetical 4.5%, the gap is $598.50 for a filer at California's top state rate and nothing at all for a filer in Texas. Run the same relationship backwards and it produces a threshold: to draw level, a CD has to pay the bill's rate divided by one minus the state rate. At the top California bracket that means beating the bill by roughly 69 basis points before the CD is worth choosing.

The rest of the comparison has nothing to do with tax and pulls in other directions. A CD arrives with a rate disclosed before the account opens and $250,000 of federal insurance behind it. The bill's rate is set at auction, nothing insures it, and no coverage ceiling applies, because the obligation belongs to the government doing the insuring. Three ordinary situations cancel the tax argument outright.

## Where the exemption is written

Publication 550 sets up the exemption by first saying what these securities are: "Treasury bills, notes, and bonds are direct debts (obligations) of the U.S. government." The tax treatment follows immediately under the heading "Taxation of interest," and the sentence does two jobs at once: it confirms the federal tax and removes the state one. "Interest income from Treasury bills, notes, and bonds is subject to federal income tax but is exempt from all state and local income taxes. You should receive Form 1099-INT showing the interest (in box 3) paid to you for the year."

That box number is the mechanical tell. Publication 550 describes it directly: "Form 1099-INT, box 3 shows the interest income you received from U.S. savings bonds, Treasury bills, Treasury notes, and Treasury bonds." Bank interest (savings, money market, CD) lands in box 1 instead. A single 1099-INT can carry both, and a state return that starts from federal taxable income is where the two boxes stop being interchangeable.

Nothing in the exemption touches the federal side. The same publication lists, under taxable interest, that "Interest on U.S. obligations, such as U.S. Treasury bills, notes, and bonds, and obligations issued by any agency or instrumentality of the United States is taxable for federal income tax purposes." A saver in a state with no income tax gets nothing from the exemption, because there was no state tax to exempt.

Two boundaries first. The exemption covers state and local income tax, not every state levy. And whether it survives being held indirectly, through a fund that owns bills rather than the bills themselves, is a matter of state law and fund reporting, not something the federal sources above settle. The case used throughout here is a bill held directly. The broader picture of what taxes do to a quoted yield is in [The Tax Bite on Savings Interest: What Your Real Yield Is](/2026/08/26/the-tax-bite-on-savings-interest-what-your-real-yield-is/).

## The after-tax gap and the break-even rate

Hold the rate constant to isolate the effect. Take $100,000 for one year, a bill and a CD both yielding a hypothetical 4.5%, and $4,500 of interest either way. Assume a federal marginal rate of 22% and a filer taking the standard deduction, so no federal offset for state tax enters the picture.

| State marginal rate | State tax on the CD interest | CD, after tax | Bill, after tax | Bill advantage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0% | $0.00 | $3,510.00 | $3,510.00 | $0.00 |
| 5% | $225.00 | $3,285.00 | $3,510.00 | $225.00 |
| 9.3% | $418.50 | $3,091.50 | $3,510.00 | $418.50 |
| 10.9% | $490.50 | $3,019.50 | $3,510.00 | $490.50 |
| 13.3% | $598.50 | $2,911.50 | $3,510.00 | $598.50 |

The last column is the second column. That is the whole result: the advantage is the state tax the CD pays and the bill does not, dollar for dollar, with no interaction effects to model.

The bracket figures at the bottom of that table are real ceilings rather than typical rates. [Tax Foundation](https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/state-income-tax-rates-2026/) data as of February 11, 2026 puts California's top marginal individual rate at 13.30 percent, applying to single-filer taxable income above $1,000,000, and New York's at 10.90 percent on income above $25,000,000. Most savers sit well below both. They are in the table for scale: even at those brackets the exemption is worth about 13 cents and 11 cents on the dollar of interest, and for the great majority of filers considerably less.

The table leaves out one complication on purpose. A filer who itemizes and deducts state income tax federally recovers part of it, narrowing the bill's advantage by whatever that deduction is worth on that particular return — a question for a tax professional rather than a general table.

Inverted, the same relationship names a threshold. If the bill yields *t* and the state taxes interest at *s*, a CD paying *c* matches it after state tax when *c* × (1 − *s*) = *t*, so the required CD rate is *t* ÷ (1 − *s*). That quotient is the taxable-equivalent yield of the bill, and the difference between it and *t* is the premium a bank has to offer before its CD is competitive.

| State marginal rate | CD rate needed to match a 4.5% bill (percent) | Premium over the bill |
|---|---|---|
| 0% | 4.50 | none |
| 5% | 4.74 | about 24 basis points |
| 9.3% | 4.96 | about 46 basis points |
| 10.9% | 5.05 | about 55 basis points |
| 13.3% | 5.19 | about 69 basis points |

The premium grows faster than the state rate does, because the denominator shrinks as the rate climbs. At the top California bracket the flip is easy to locate: a CD at 5% keeps 5 × (1 − 0.133) = 4.335 after state tax, short of the bill, while a CD at 5.2% keeps 4.508 and clears it. Somewhere near 5.19 the two are indifferent, and every basis point above that belongs to the CD. In a state with no income tax the threshold is the bill's own rate, so a CD at 4.6% wins and a CD at 4.4% loses, with nothing else to calculate.

The inputs have to match. A bill's return is quoted both as a discount rate and as a coupon-equivalent yield, and only the second sits on the same footing as a CD's annual percentage yield. Comparing the wrong pair quietly hands one side a headline it did not earn. That discipline applies to two bank offers, covered in [Six Lines in a Bank Disclosure That Decide What You Earn](/2026/08/24/six-lines-in-a-bank-disclosure-that-decide-what-you-earn/).

## What the two curves actually pay

In practice the two instruments have not been quoted at the same number, and the gap has been too wide for any state exemption to decide it. Treasury's daily bill rates for [September 18, 2026](https://home.treasury.gov/resource-center/data-chart-center/interest-rates/TextView?type=daily_treasury_bill_rates), stated as coupon equivalents, against the FDIC national average CD rates published as of August 17, 2026:

| Bill term | Coupon equivalent, Sept 18, 2026 (percent) | FDIC national average CD (percent) | Gap in percentage points |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 weeks | 3.89 | 1 month, 0.22 | 3.67 |
| 8 weeks | 4.00 | — | — |
| 13 weeks | 4.08 | 3 month, 1.14 | 2.94 |
| 17 weeks | 4.13 | — | — |
| 26 weeks | 4.27 | 6 month, 1.41 | 2.86 |
| 52 weeks | 4.41 | 12 month, 1.71 | 2.70 |

The two columns are dated about a month apart, so the gaps are indicative rather than a clean same-day snapshot. Even allowing for that, an exemption worth at most about two-thirds of a percentage point at the top California bracket does not close a gap of 2.7 points. The tax break is a tiebreaker at the competitive end of the CD market, not the main event against the average.

The averages sit that low because the [FDIC](https://www.fdic.gov/national-rates-and-rate-caps) national rate is "the average of rates paid by all insured depository institutions and credit unions for which data is available, with rates weighted by each institution's share of domestic deposits." Thousands of institutions paying nearly nothing drag the figure down. The FDIC's companion number tells the same story from the other side. The national rate cap is "the higher of: (1) the national rate plus 75 basis points; or (2) 120 percent of the current yield on similar maturity U.S. Department of the Treasury obligations plus 75 basis points." On August 17, 2026 the 12-month average was 1.71% and the matching cap 5.65 percent, a spread that opens only because the second leg of the formula is a Treasury calculation rather than a deposit one. Even the bank regulator benchmarks the top of the deposit market against Treasury yields.

Competitive CDs are a different population from the average, and the one worth comparing. Where the best terms tend to sit on the curve is the subject of [Building a CD Ladder When 12-Month CDs Pay the Most](/2026/08/19/building-a-cd-ladder-when-12-month-cds-pay-the-most/).

## Buying a bill: terms, minimum, auction

Treasury sells bills "for terms ranging from four weeks to 52 weeks," and the glance table lists the exact set: 4, 6, 8, 13, 17, 26, and 52 weeks. Cash management bills run at other terms but "are only available through a bank, broker, or dealer. We do not sell them in TreasuryDirect."

The purchase mechanics differ from opening a CD in ways that matter more than the paperwork suggests.

- **Minimum and increments.** "$100" minimum, "In increments of $100." Nothing about a bill requires a large balance, which is the opposite of the tiered-minimum structure many CD rate sheets use.
- **Maximum.** "$10 million (non-competitive bid)" per auction, or "35% of offering amount (competitive bid)."
- **Pricing.** "Bills are sold at a discount or at par (face value). When the bill matures, you are paid its face value." There is no periodic interest payment; the glance table's interest-paid row reads "When the bill matures."
- **Schedule.** "Weekly for 4, 6, 8, 13, 17, 26-week bills" and "Every four weeks for 52-week bills."

The largest difference is the one savers notice last. [TreasuryDirect](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/buying-a-marketable-security/) is explicit: "When you schedule the purchase of a marketable security in TreasuryDirect, you don't know the interest rate. The interest rate is determined at auction." A non-competitive bid, the only kind TreasuryDirect accepts, trades certainty of rate for certainty of fill: "you are guaranteed to get the security you want in the amount you want" and "you agree to accept the discount (high) rate, (high) yield, or (high) discount margin determined at auction." A CD does the reverse: the APY is disclosed before the account is funded and fixed for the term.

Getting back out has a floor on it. New purchases through TreasuryDirect carry a lockup — "you must hold new Treasury marketable securities for at least 45 calendar days before transferring or selling them," though that holding period does not apply when a security is bought with proceeds from a reinvestment.

Rolling a bill is scheduled in advance rather than renewed automatically the way a CD is. [Reinvestments](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/reinvesting-a-marketable-security/) can be set "when you buy the original security or at any time up to four business days before the original security matures," and a bill must roll into the same term: "you can reinvest a maturing 52-week bill only in another 52-week bill." The number of rolls is capped, because "bills may be scheduled for multiple reinvestments, up to two years":

| Bill term | Maximum scheduled reinvestments |
|---|---|
| 4-week | 25 |
| 6-week | 16 |
| 8-week | 10 |
| 13-week | 7 |
| 17-week | 6 |
| 26-week | 3 |
| 52-week | 1 |

Two failure modes come with that. The window closes early — "We close the option to reinvest four business days before the relevant auction." A roll can also cost more than the maturing bill returns, in which case "if funds are not available to pay the difference, we will cancel the reinvestment and deposit the proceeds of the maturing security into your bank account or C of I." A CD that auto-renews does none of this; it simply renews, which is a hazard of another kind.

## Insurance against credit

The second real difference is what stands behind the money, and the two answers are not the same kind of answer.

A CD is a deposit. [FDIC deposit insurance](https://www.fdic.gov/resources/deposit-insurance/understanding-deposit-insurance/) "covers $250,000 per depositor, per FDIC-insured bank, for each account ownership category," and the record behind it is why the coverage is taken for granted: "Since the FDIC was founded in 1933, no depositor has lost a penny of FDIC-insured funds." The insurance is a promise about a bank's failure, capped in dollars and counted per bank and per ownership category.

A bill is not insured and does not need to be. It is, in Publication 550's phrasing, a direct debt of the U.S. government — the same government that stands behind the insurance fund. There is no $250,000 line because there is no third party whose failure the coverage is meant to survive.

Where that distinction stops being academic is above the insurance limit. A $600,000 cash position in CDs has to be spread across banks, ownership categories, or a deposit network to stay fully covered; the same $600,000 in bills raises no coverage question at all. The mechanics of stretching coverage are in [Insuring More Than $250,000 Without Opening Ten Accounts](/2026/09/02/insuring-more-than-250000-without-opening-ten-accounts/) and [How FDIC Ownership Categories Stack Coverage at One Bank](/2026/08/21/how-fdic-ownership-categories-stack-coverage-at-one-bank/).

One trap sits between the two. The FDIC's list of what it does not insure includes "Stocks and Bonds," and that list applies inside an insured bank's own brokerage. A Treasury bill bought through a bank is not a deposit of that bank, and a brokered CD is a different instrument again, with its own secondary-market pricing. Those distinctions are worked through in [Brokered CDs vs Bank CDs: The Differences That Matter](/2026/08/27/brokered-cds-vs-bank-cds-the-differences-that-matter/) and [Where Brokerage Cash Actually Sits and What Insures It](/2026/08/30/where-brokerage-cash-actually-sits-and-what-insures-it/).

## One instrument, two tax years

The exemption changes how much tax is owed. The reporting rules change when it is owed, and a bill bought late in a calendar year can push an entire year of interest onto the following return.

Publication 550 sets the default for bills: "The difference between the discounted price you pay for the bills and the face value you receive at maturity is interest income. Generally, you report this interest income when the bill is paid at maturity." A 52-week bill issued in November therefore puts its entire year of income into the following tax year. A CD's timing depends on how the bank pays it. Publication 550 brings deferred-account interest into income "when you actually receive it or are entitled to receive it without paying a substantial penalty," and adds that "the same is true for accounts that mature in 1 year or less and pay interest in a single payment at maturity." A CD crediting interest monthly or quarterly therefore splits the income across both calendar years, while one paying a single sum at maturity does not. What gets reported is gross in either case: a depositor charged an early-withdrawal penalty "must report the total amount of interest paid or credited to your account during the year without subtracting the penalty."

The default is not mandatory. "When you buy a short-term obligation (one with a fixed maturity date of 1 year or less from the date of issue), other than a tax-exempt obligation, you generally can choose to include any discount and interest payable on the obligation in income currently." For a short-term government obligation, the amount brought into income is "the accrued acquisition discount, if any, plus any other accrued interest payable on the obligation," with the acquisition discount defined as "the stated redemption price at maturity minus your basis." The choice is not open to everyone: current accrual is required for a short-term obligation "held by an accrual-basis taxpayer," held by a bank or regulated investment company, held primarily for sale to customers, or identified as part of a hedging transaction, among the listed cases.

Rolling bills does not push the income forward either: "you must report the full amount of the interest income on each of your Treasury bills by the time it reaches maturity." Each bill settles its own tax at its own maturity, whether the chain runs one roll or twenty-five. The same passage describes reinvestment proceeds as "par amount less any tax withheld," a reminder that withholding can reach this interest as it reaches bank interest — what triggers it and how the money comes back is in [Backup Withholding on Savings Interest: Why the Bank Took 24%](/2026/09/21/backup-withholding-on-savings-interest-why-the-bank-took-24/).

## A disclosed penalty against a market price

Both instruments can be exited early, at costs of different shapes.

Breaking a CD has a price written down before the account is opened, and the tax code partly refunds it. Publication 550: "If you withdraw funds from a certificate of deposit or other deferred interest account before maturity, you may be charged a penalty. The Form 1099-INT or similar statement given to you by the financial institution will show the total amount of interest in box 1 and will show the penalty separately in box 2. You must include in income all interest shown in Form 1099-INT, box 1. You can deduct the penalty on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 18." The number is knowable in advance, and the deduction sits in the adjustments section, so it does not require itemizing. The disclosure rules behind that penalty are in [CD Early Withdrawal Penalties: The Disclosure and the Deduction](/2026/09/22/cd-early-withdrawal-penalties-the-disclosure-and-the-deduction/), and the arithmetic of whether to break one is in [When Breaking a CD Actually Pays: Run the Break-Even](/2026/08/25/when-breaking-a-cd-actually-pays-run-the-break-even/).

Selling a bill has no penalty and no fixed price. The bills page states the option in one line: "You can hold a bill until it matures or sell it before it matures." What the sale returns goes unmentioned, because that is a market question. Sold before maturity, a bill settles at whatever the market pays that day, which can be above or below what was paid for it. And for the first 45 calendar days after a new purchase in TreasuryDirect, no sale is possible at all.

That inverts the usual intuition about which instrument is easier to leave. A CD's worst case is a disclosed number, fixed when the account opens, that can reach into principal. A bill's worst case before maturity is bounded by nothing but the price on the screen — and at maturity there is no bad case, since face value is paid in full.

Enter the two rates, a state bracket, and a balance to see the after-tax comparison.

{% include tools/after-tax-real-return.html %}

## Where the comparison flips back

The tax argument is conditional. Three situations switch it off.

**No state income tax to avoid.** Tax Foundation's 2026 data counts eight states that "levy no individual income tax at all": Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas and Wyoming. New Hampshire counts because it "repealed its interest and dividends tax as of 2025." In those states the taxable-equivalent yield equals the bill's own rate, the second table above collapses to its first row, and the decision reverts to whichever headline number is larger.

**A CD premium above the break-even.** Competitive CDs are priced by institutions competing for deposits, not by the Treasury market, and the gap between the best CD and the bill curve is not fixed. Whenever a CD clears *t* ÷ (1 − *s*), the exemption has been out-bid, and the CD wins on after-tax yield while also carrying insurance and a rate that was disclosed rather than auctioned.

**A tax-deferred account.** Inside an IRA, interest is not being taxed currently, so exempting it from a state tax nobody is charging is worth nothing. A bill held in an IRA gives up the CD's disclosed rate and gains nothing in return on the tax side. The retirement-account wrinkles are in [IRA CDs: Insurance, Rollovers, and the RMD Deadline](/2026/09/12/ira-cds-insurance-rollovers-and-the-rmd-deadline/).

Two smaller cases push the same way. A saver whose state taxable income is low enough that the interest is effectively untaxed sits in the first situation without living in one of those states. Anyone who might need the money before maturity has reason to prefer a cost printed in a disclosure to a price set by a market.

## Common questions

**Is Treasury bill interest exempt from federal tax too?** No. Publication 550 lists interest on U.S. obligations under taxable interest and states that bill, note and bond interest "is subject to federal income tax but is exempt from all state and local income taxes." The exemption is state and local only.

**How does the tax difference show up on the forms?** By box. Publication 550: "Form 1099-INT, box 3 shows the interest income you received from U.S. savings bonds, Treasury bills, Treasury notes, and Treasury bonds." Bank interest, including CD interest, is reported in box 1 of the same form.

**What does it take to buy a bill?** The minimum is $100, in $100 increments, with a non-competitive maximum of $10 million per auction. Bills "are sold at a discount or at par (face value)," and no interest is paid until maturity. In TreasuryDirect the rate is unknown when the purchase is scheduled, because it is set at auction.

**Can a Treasury bill be cashed early like a CD?** Not in the same way. TreasuryDirect states that a bill can be held to maturity or sold before it matures, and that new purchases there must be held "for at least 45 calendar days before transferring or selling them." An early sale settles at a market price rather than a penalty formula, so the cost is not knowable in advance the way a CD's is.

**Is a Treasury bill FDIC insured?** No, and the question has the wrong shape. FDIC insurance covers "$250,000 per depositor, per FDIC-insured bank, for each account ownership category" and applies to deposits at banks; the FDIC's own list of uninsured products includes stocks and bonds. A bill is a direct obligation of the U.S. government rather than a deposit at an institution that could fail. Confirming an institution's insured status before a transfer is covered in [How to Verify a Bank Is Actually FDIC Insured Before You Transfer](/2026/09/09/how-to-verify-a-bank-is-actually-fdic-insured-before-you-transfer/).

The exemption is worth exactly one number: the state marginal rate applied to the interest. That number decides the comparison only where the two quotes already sit close together. Against the 12-month national average of 1.71% the headline gap settles it first, and in eight states the number is zero.

title: I Bonds vs a High-Yield Savings Account: The 12-Month Lock
description: The composite rate is published and the 0.90% fixed half is permanent, but the money is unreachable for 12 months and cashing before five years forfeits three months of interest.
content:
The savings account holds $18,400 at an APY a rounding error away from the FDIC national average for savings, 0.38% as of August 17, 2026. A year of that is about $70. A Treasury page then quotes 4.26%, and the plan writes itself: empty the savings account into I bonds on Monday.

Three lines on that same Treasury page close the door on that version of the plan. [TreasuryDirect](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/savings-bonds/i-bonds/) sets the holding rule — "You can cash in (redeem) your I bond after 12 months." The exit cost: "if you cash in the bond in less than 5 years, you lose the last 3 months of interest." And the annual ceiling runs to "up to $10,000 in electronic I bonds" per Social Security Number in a calendar year, so $18,400 does not fit in one year no matter how the decision goes.

None of that makes the 4.26% wrong. It applies to bonds "issued May 1, 2026 to October 31, 2026," and the arithmetic behind it is published. What it makes wrong is the category. An I bond is a 30-year Treasury security with a year of complete ineligibility at the front and a penalty tail running to year five. A savings account is money that reaches a plumber this afternoon. Swapping one for the other changes what the money can do, and the account being emptied is usually the one the household relied on to absorb a surprise.

The second thing hidden in that date range is a deadline savers read backwards. A new rate is announced every November 1, and the late-October question is always whether the headline will rise or fall. That is the half of the rate that resets on a six-month clock no matter when the bond is bought. The half genuinely decided by buying before October 31 is the fixed rate, which attaches to the bond permanently.

## The composite rate and its two halves

The 4.26% is not a rate anyone chose. TreasuryDirect publishes the arithmetic as a formula, brackets and all: "Composite rate formula: [Fixed rate + (2 x semiannual inflation rate) + (fixed rate x semiannual inflation rate)]." The Treasury's [May 1, 2026 announcement](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/news/2026/release-05-01-rates/) gives the two inputs, describing the result as combining "a 0.90% fixed rate of return with the 3.34% annualized rate of inflation." Run those through the formula the way [TreasuryDirect's own worked example](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/savings-bonds/i-bonds/i-bonds-interest-rates/) does, as [0.0090 + (2 x 0.0167) + (0.0090 x 0.0167)], and 4.26% falls out.

The two halves behave nothing alike, and conflating them is where most I bond reasoning goes wrong.

The fixed rate is permanent. TreasuryDirect says it "never changes" and spells out how it is assigned: "We announce the fixed rate every May 1 and November 1. That fixed rate then applies, for the life of the bond, to all I bonds that we issue during the next 6 months." A bond bought in September 2026 carries 0.90% in the first slot of that formula through every future recalculation, all the way to year 30.

The inflation half runs on a clock. "The inflation rate changes every 6 months. We set the inflation rate every May 1 and November 1." Whatever is announced on November 1 replaces the current figure for every outstanding I bond eventually, regardless of when it was purchased. Nobody escapes an inflation reset by buying early, and nobody captures one by buying late.

A floor sits underneath the combination. TreasuryDirect: "if the inflation rate is so negative that it would pull the combined rate below zero, we don't let that happen. We stop at zero." A stretch of deflation stops the bond earning rather than shrinking what it is worth. A savings account has no equivalent published rule; what it has instead is a bank's discretion to reprice, which moves in one direction faster than the other, as covered in [Why Your Savings Rate Drops Faster Than It Rises](/2026/09/01/deposit-betas-why-savings-rates-fall-faster-than-they-rise/).

Accrual and compounding run on separate clocks. Both series "earn interest monthly. Interest is compounded semiannually," and TreasuryDirect describes the mechanic directly: "Twice a year, we add all the interest the bond earned in the previous 6 months to the main (principal) value of the bond... Over the next 6 months, we apply the new interest rate to that entire new value."

So the headline is an annual rate applied in six-month pieces. On $10,000 bought at 4.26%, the first six months add half of that composite, about $213, leaving the bond worth roughly $10,213 at the end of the first rate period. What the second six months adds is unknown on the day of purchase. This is the part the comparison with a savings APY quietly drops: only the first six months of the number are on offer.

## Twelve months, and the one documented exception

The lock is absolute and stated in one sentence: "You can cash in (redeem) your I bond after 12 months."

That is the sharpest structural difference from a certificate of deposit, which gets lumped in with it as "locked money." A CD is not locked. A CD has a price, which federal deposit rules require the bank to put in writing before the account is opened, stating "how it is calculated, and the conditions for its assessment," as worked through in [CD Early Withdrawal Penalties: The Disclosure and the Deduction](/2026/09/22/cd-early-withdrawal-penalties-the-disclosure-and-the-deduction/). An I bond in month seven has no price. The request cannot be made.

One documented exception exists. TreasuryDirect's page for bondholders affected by a disaster says bonds can be cashed "Even if they are less than a year old," and adds the parenthetical that explains why the line is there at all: "(Normally, bonds can't be cashed in their first year.)" Eligibility turns on living in "an area that has had an official disaster declaration," which is checked against FEMA's list rather than described to a customer service representative. A declared disaster is not the same category of event as a transmission failing.

The dating runs slightly in the buyer's favor. "I bonds earn interest from the first day of the month you buy them," so a purchase made on October 28 collects the whole of October. It does not shorten the year of ineligibility.

After the year is up, the bond does not have to be cashed whole. TreasuryDirect permits redeeming "Any amount of $25 or more to the penny," with two conditions: "If you cash only part of what a bond is worth, you must leave at least $25 in your account," and "If you cash only part of what a bond is worth, you only get the interest on the part you cash." That is cleaner than a partial CD withdrawal, which can reprice the balance left behind, and it is available only after the twelve months have run.

The consequence is definitional. An emergency fund is the money available in the week something breaks, not the money that earns the most over a year, and anything with a twelve-month ineligibility window fails that test by construction. That is a different objection from calling it a bad investment. The layering question is covered in [A Beginner's Guide to Creating an Emergency Fund With Different Financial Products](/2026/08/17/a-beginners-guide-to-creating-an-emergency-fund-with-different-financial-products/), and the separate confusion about how freely a savings account can be tapped is in [The Savings Withdrawal Limit Was Repealed. Your Bank Kept It Anyway](/2026/09/10/the-savings-withdrawal-limit-was-repealed-your-bank-kept-it-anyway/).

## The three-month forfeiture in dollars

The second cost is quoted in time, not money: "if you cash in the bond in less than 5 years, you lose the last 3 months of interest." Converting that into dollars is the only way to see how much of the headline it takes.

TreasuryDirect nets the forfeiture out of the number on screen: for bonds under five years old, the values shown in the account and in the savings bond calculator already exclude the last three months of interest. The balance a holder sees at month fourteen is what would actually arrive. That removes one unpleasant surprise and creates another: the account appears to stall for a quarter after every purchase.

Take a $10,000 bond bought at 4.26%. The illustration holds the composite constant across every period, which will not happen in reality, since only 0.90% of it is fixed. Holding it constant isolates what the forfeiture costs rather than blending it with an inflation guess.

| Cashed at | Value at a constant 4.26% | Three months forfeited | Net proceeds | Annualized |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 months | $10,430.54 | about $108.77 | about $10,321.77 | about 3.2% |
| 24 months | $10,879.61 | about $113.45 | about $10,766.16 | about 3.8% |
| 60 months | $12,346.20 | none | $12,346.20 | about 4.3% |

Three readings come out of that table.

The forfeiture is not a flat fee. It is three months of whatever the bond is earning at the time, on whatever the bond is worth at the time, so the dollar figure grows while its proportional bite shrinks. On a bond cashed at the earliest possible moment it takes roughly a quarter of everything earned.

The minimum-hold case is the honest comparison. A saver who holds exactly the twelve months required is not buying 4.26%. Under this illustration they are buying something closer to three and a quarter percent, for money that was unreachable throughout. Against a competitive savings account that stayed liquid, that is a narrower contest than the headline suggests, and it can lose outright if the second six-month rate comes in low.

The penalty disappears at five years, which is also the point at which the horizon has stopped resembling a savings account at all. Savers who want it gone without the wait are describing a [no-penalty CD](/2026/08/28/no-penalty-bump-up-and-add-on-cds-when-the-variants-pay/), which trades rate for exactly that.

## The $10,000 ceiling per Social Security Number

The limit is stated per person, per year, per series: "In any one calendar year for one Social Security Number, you may buy up to: $10,000 in electronic EE bonds [and] $10,000 in electronic I bonds." The two are separate buckets, not a shared cap. At the other end, "You can buy an electronic savings bond for any amount from $25 to $10,000 to the penny," so there is no meaningful minimum.

The paper route people remember from tax season is closed. TreasuryDirect states it flatly: "As of January 1, 2025, all new I bonds are electronic." The tax-refund purchase that once allowed an extra allocation in paper form is no longer an available answer to the ceiling.

Who can hold them is broader than the per-SSN framing implies. The owner "must have a Social Security Number" and be a "United States citizen," "United States resident," or "Civilian employee of the United States." Beyond that, "You may also register the bond in the name of a trust or estate. An electronic bond in TreasuryDirect also can be in the name of a corporation, partnership, or other entity." A minor can hold them, with the qualifier that "The child needs a TreasuryDirect account that is linked to the account of a parent or other adult custodian" — a structure with its own tax consequences, set out in [Savings Accounts for Kids: Custodial Rules and the Kiddie Tax](/2026/09/17/savings-accounts-for-kids-custodial-rules-and-the-kiddie-tax/).

The phrase carrying the most weight is "in any one calendar year." The allowance does not accrue and does not roll forward. An allowance unused on December 31 is gone, and two purchases six weeks apart, one in late December and one in early January, draw on two separate years. That is the only lever that moves the ceiling without adding a second person or entity.

Run the ceiling against a real cash position and the shape becomes obvious. A household spending $5,000 a month with a six-month buffer is holding $30,000. Converting that takes three calendar years at $10,000 a year for one SSN, and each tranche is separately unreachable for its own twelve months. That describes a ladder, with rungs opening in sequence, rather than a pile of accessible cash — the same reasoning applied to deposits is in [Building a CD Ladder When 12-Month CDs Pay the Most](/2026/08/19/building-a-cd-ladder-when-12-month-cds-pay-the-most/).

## What the savings side actually pays

The other half of the comparison is usually supplied by a headline rather than a statement, and the FDIC publishes two different numbers that get mixed up constantly.

The first is the national average. The FDIC's Monthly Rate Cap Information as of August 17, 2026 puts savings at 0.38%, money market accounts at 0.63%, and the 12-month CD at 1.71%. The methodology is stated on the same page: these are "The average of rates paid by all insured depository institutions and credit unions for which data is available, with rates weighted by each institution's share of domestic deposits." Weighting by deposit share is what makes the savings figure so low: the largest deposit books belong to branch networks that never repriced.

The second is the rate cap, a supervisory ceiling rather than a market observation. The FDIC sets it as "the higher of: (1) the national rate plus 75 basis points; or (2) 120 percent of the current yield on similar maturity U.S. Department of the Treasury (U.S. Treasury) obligations plus 75 basis points." On the same August table, that formula puts the savings cap above four percent, more than ten times the average printed beside it. No bank is obliged to pay the cap and it is not an offer to anyone. What it reveals is that the regulator's own arithmetic assumes deposit rates well above the deposit-weighted average are ordinary.

Which is the practical point. The comparison worth running is not 4.26% against 0.38%. It is 4.26% against the APY printed on the statement of the account the money would leave. The FDIC does not publish what competitive online institutions pay, and the gap between a repriced online account and a legacy branch account is often larger than the gap between either of them and an I bond. A saver who has not looked up their own APY is comparing a verified Treasury figure against a blank.

A savings account is an insured deposit, covered to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category, with the stacking rules described in [Common Mistakes With Understanding FDIC Insurance Limits and How to Avoid Them](/2026/08/18/common-mistakes-with-understanding-fdic-insurance-limits-and-how-to-avoid-them/). An I bond is not a deposit and is not FDIC-insured. It is a Treasury obligation recorded in a TreasuryDirect account, so the per-bank limits neither cover it nor are consumed by it.

## The November 1 reset and the October 31 question

Now the date on the front of the page. Two separate decisions hide inside "buy before October 31."

An October purchase locks one thing permanently. The fixed rate is 0.90% and it attaches to the bond for life. Every future composite the bond earns, in 2031 and in 2051, is computed with 0.90% sitting in the first slot of the formula. A bond bought on November 1 or later carries whatever fixed rate is announced that morning, also for life. This is the only part of the decision with permanent consequences, and it does not appear in the headline number.

The other decision is when the reset reaches a particular bond, and the answer is not November 1. TreasuryDirect schedules rate changes by issue month, not by announcement date. A bond issued in October has its rates change on "April 1 and October 1." A bond issued in November changes on "May 1 and November 1." Every month of the year has its own pair.

Follow that through. A bond bought in October 2026 earns 4.26% from October 1, 2026 through the end of March 2027, and picks up the rate announced on November 1, 2026 only from April 1, 2027. A bond bought in November 2026 takes the newly announced number immediately, for its first six months.

Restated: the October buyer gets six months at a published rate and then runs six months behind the announcement calendar. The November buyer takes the new number straight away, better or worse, and locks the new fixed rate for life. Both receive every future inflation adjustment.

So the question that matters is not whether the headline will be higher or lower on November 1. It is two narrower questions. Is a known 4.26% for the next six months preferable to an unknown figure for the same six months? And is 0.90% fixed for thirty years better than the fixed rate the Treasury announces that day, which nobody outside the announcement knows in advance?

A forecast of the inflation half is not the input people think it is. TreasuryDirect describes it as changing "every 6 months, based on inflation," a calculation applied to published data rather than a judgment call, and it reaches the bond on schedule regardless of purchase month. The fixed rate is the discretionary piece, and it is the one that cannot be revisited.

Sitting under both questions is the calendar year. October and November purchases both consume the 2026 allowance; the difference between them is six months of rate timing on at most $10,000. A purchase pushed into January consumes 2027's allowance and leaves 2026's unused permanently, which moves more money than the reset debate does.

## The tax line that runs the other way

Interest on an I bond is taxed at one level. TreasuryDirect's comparison table reads "Federal income tax: Yes. State and local income tax: No." Interest on a savings account is taxed at every level that taxes income where the depositor lives.

Timing is the larger structural difference, and it is elective. A holder may "put off (defer) reporting the interest until you file a federal income tax return for the year in which you actually get the interest," or instead "report the interest each year even though you don't actually get the interest then." Most holders take the first option by default.

Savings interest has no such choice. It is credited monthly, reported annually, and taxed annually, so a portion of every year's yield leaves before it can compound. An I bond held under the cash method produces no federal tax event at all until it is cashed. The paperwork follows the cash: "You get a Form 1099-INT for the year in which you get the interest," and for electronic holdings "your 1099-INT is available in your account by January 31 of the following year."

Two consequences follow, and they run opposite ways.

Deferral compounds gross. Every dollar of interest that would have gone to tax in a savings account stays in the bond earning the composite rate for the rest of the holding period, so the after-tax gap between the two products is wider than the stated rate gap. The mechanics of that drag on a taxable account are worked through in [The Tax Bite on Savings Interest: What Your Real Yield Is](/2026/08/26/the-tax-bite-on-savings-interest-what-your-real-yield-is/).

Deferral also concentrates. Years of accrued interest land in a single return in the year of redemption, which can push the total into a worse bracket than a long string of small annual amounts would have occupied. Anyone with a choice about when to trigger a large redemption is making a bracket decision, not only a rate decision, and the annual-reporting election exists partly for that reason.

The state exemption is worth more than it looks in a high-tax state. At a hypothetical 5% state rate, a fully taxable account has to pay roughly 4.5% to leave the same amount in hand as a 4.26% instrument exempt from state tax, before any federal interactions.

An education exclusion sits off to one side of this comparison. TreasuryDirect notes that "Using the money for higher education may keep you from paying federal income tax on your savings bond interest," and routes the eligibility rules and income restrictions to a separate page. A tax professional is the right check on how any of this lands on a particular return.

## Where each one sits

The two products are not competing for the same dollar, which is why the head-to-head framing keeps producing bad answers.

Money that might be needed this week has one home, and the rate on it is secondary. Past twelve months, an I bond, a term deposit, or a mix all come into range, and there the comparison is genuine: 4.26% for six months and an unknown rate after, against the FDIC average of 1.71% for a 12-month CD as of August 17, 2026 or whatever a competitive institution posts. At five years the I bond's structure stops costing anything — the forfeiture has expired, the deferral has had room to compound, and the fixed rate is still working.

The headline comparison fails because the two rates are set by different things. A bank's savings APY is a pricing decision, revisable at the bank's convenience, which is why it can fall the week after it was checked. The I bond's composite is an announcement on a published schedule. Comparing them at a single instant treats both as fixed, and neither one is.

## Common questions

**Can an I bond be cashed before twelve months if the money is needed?** No, outside one documented exception. The rule is "You can cash in (redeem) your I bond after 12 months," and TreasuryDirect's disaster page is the only route around it, allowing redemption "Even if they are less than a year old" for holders in "an area that has had an official disaster declaration." There is no hardship provision and no fee that buys an early exit.

**Does the three-month forfeiture apply at exactly five years?** The wording is "if you cash in the bond in less than 5 years, you lose the last 3 months of interest," so at five years and beyond it stops. Before that point, note that TreasuryDirect already subtracts it from the value displayed for bonds under five years old, so the balance on screen is what would actually be paid.

**Can a couple buy $20,000 in one year?** The limit is written per Social Security Number: "In any one calendar year for one Social Security Number, you may buy up to: $10,000 in electronic EE bonds [and] $10,000 in electronic I bonds." Two people with two SSNs and two TreasuryDirect accounts each have their own I bond allowance, and the EE allowance sits alongside it rather than inside it. Trusts, estates, corporations and partnerships can also be registered owners.

**What happens to an I bond if inflation turns negative?** TreasuryDirect caps the downside: "if the inflation rate is so negative that it would pull the combined rate below zero, we don't let that happen. We stop at zero." A deflationary stretch stops the bond earning for that period rather than reducing what it is worth, and the fixed rate stays attached throughout.

**Do I bonds use up FDIC coverage at a bank?** No. They are Treasury securities recorded in a TreasuryDirect account rather than deposits at an insured institution, so the $250,000 per-depositor, per-bank, per-ownership-category limits neither cover them nor are consumed by them.

Every number on the Treasury side of this comparison is published: 4.26% for bonds issued through October 31, 0.90% fixed for the life of those bonds, twelve months before redemption is possible, three months of interest forfeited before year five, $10,000 per Social Security Number per calendar year. The number on the other side is not published anywhere, because it is specific to one account at one bank. It is on the statement, and it is the only half of this comparison a saver has to go looking for.

**Sources:** [TreasuryDirect — Series I Savings Bonds](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/savings-bonds/i-bonds/) · [TreasuryDirect — I bonds interest rates](https://www.treasurydirect.gov/savings-bonds/i-bonds/i-bonds-interest-rates/) · [FDIC — National Rates and Rate Caps](https://www.fdic.gov/national-rates-and-rate-caps)

title: Why You Owe Tax on a 5-Year CD You Cannot Touch Yet
description: A multi-year CD that pays everything at maturity still produces taxable income every year. Form 1099-OID, the constructive receipt rule, and where the cash to pay the tax comes from.
content:
The Form 1099-OID arrives in the last week of January. Box 1 shows a figure in four digits. The CD it refers to was opened in 2024, matures in 2029, and has paid out nothing at all — no transfer, no check, no line on a checking statement. The balance shown in online banking cannot be reduced by a dollar without triggering the early withdrawal clause. The amount in Box 1 is taxable income for the year that just ended, and the tax on it is due in April, in cash the CD does not provide.

The form is correct. What decides this is not whether the money can be reached but how long the interest is deferred, and the dividing line sits at one year. [IRS Publication 550](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550) puts it in two sentences under *Certificates of deposit and other deferred interest accounts*: "You generally must include this interest in your income when you actually receive it or are entitled to receive it without paying a substantial penalty. The same is true for accounts that mature in 1 year or less and pay interest in a single payment at maturity." Then the pivot: "If interest is deferred for more than 1 year, see Original Issue Discount (OID), later."

Three things follow. A multi-year CD that holds all of its interest until maturity is treated as a discounted debt instrument, producing income every year of its term whether or not anything is paid out. That income arrives on Form 1099-OID rather than Form 1099-INT, and the two forms report different things in nearly identical boxes. And the tax has to be funded from somewhere else, because the only account that earned the money is the one that will not release it.

The alternative is a CD that pays interest out monthly. It earns less in total, since nothing compounds inside the account, but every dollar of tax it creates arrives alongside cash to pay it with. Which of the two is worth more after five years is arithmetic, and the answer is closer than the yield difference suggests.

## The rule that decides which form arrives

Two separate rules are at work, and they meet at the crediting schedule.

The first is constructive receipt, stated in Publication 550 as a general principle before it is applied to deposits: "You constructively receive income when it is credited to your account or made available to you. You do not need to have physical possession of it. For example, you are considered to receive interest, dividends, or other earnings on any deposit or account in a bank, savings and loan association, or similar financial institution ... when they are credited to your account and subject to your withdrawal."

The words "subject to your withdrawal" are doing less work than they appear to, because the same passage lists four obstacles that do not break constructive receipt. Income is still constructively received even if the depositor must:

- "Make withdrawals in multiples of even amounts,"
- "Give a notice to withdraw before making the withdrawal,"
- "Withdraw all or part of the account to withdraw the earnings, or"
- "Pay a penalty on early withdrawals, unless the interest you are to receive on an early withdrawal or redemption is substantially less than the interest payable at maturity."

The fourth bullet is the hinge for every CD. A penalty alone does not postpone the tax. The exception only opens where the interest actually payable on an early exit is "substantially less than the interest payable at maturity," which is a different and much narrower question than whether a penalty exists. A CD that credits interest annually, lets the depositor draw that credited interest out, and charges a penalty only against principal is producing taxable income each year it credits.

The second rule is the one-year deferral line already quoted. Interest "paid at fixed intervals of 1 year or less during the term of the account" is ordinary interest income, reported by the bank in Box 1 of Form 1099-INT. The [Instructions for Forms 1099-INT and 1099-OID](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099int) describe that box broadly enough to cover the whole category: "Include amounts of $10 or more, whether or not designated as interest, that are paid or credited to the person's account by savings and loan associations, mutual savings banks ... credit unions, or similar organizations."

"Paid or credited" is the operative pair. Crediting is enough. Nothing has to leave the bank.

Interest deferred past a year leaves Form 1099-INT entirely and becomes original issue discount. That is not a special rule invented for deposits — it is the same regime that governs zero coupon bonds, applied to a bank product that behaves the same way.

## Original issue discount on a bank deposit

Publication 550 opens its CD section with a six-word sentence that explains everything downstream of it: "A CD is a debt instrument."

The definition follows from that. "OID is a form of interest. You generally include OID in your income as it accrues over the term of the debt instrument, whether or not you receive any payments from the issuer." Structurally, "OID is the difference between the stated redemption price at maturity and the issue price" — so a $40,000 deposit that will return $48,666 in five years was bought at a discount to what it pays back. The presumption is stated directly: "All debt instruments that pay no interest before maturity are presumed to be issued at a discount."

The application to deposits is explicit: "If you buy a CD with a maturity of more than 1 year, you must include in income each year a part of the total interest due and report it in the same manner as other OID." And the same treatment reaches a list of products that are not always called CDs:

- Time deposits
- Bonus plans
- Savings certificates
- Deferred income certificates
- Bonus savings certificates
- Growth savings certificates

Marketing names on a rate sheet do not change the classification. What matters is the term and whether interest is deferred past a year.

The bank's filing duty is spelled out in the 1099 instructions, which require Form 1099-OID from "an issuer of a certificate of deposit (CD) made, purchased, or renewed after 1970 if the CD has OID and a term of more than 1 year." The same instructions set the reporting floor at "the total daily portions of original issue discount (OID) for a holder is at least $10" — daily portions, because OID accrues by the day rather than on a crediting date, which is why the figure on a 1099-OID for the first partial year of a CD often matches no line on any statement.

Publication 550 works a deposit example in full, under *Time deposit open account arrangement*: "you and your bank enter into an arrangement under which you agree to deposit $100 each month for a period of 5 years. Interest will be compounded twice a year at 7 1/2%, but payable only at the end of the 5-year period. You must include a part of the interest in your income as OID each year. Each year the bank must give you a Form 1099-OID to show you the amount you must include in your income for the year." The defining feature is stated one sentence earlier — "there is no actual or constructive receipt of interest until the fixed maturity date is reached" — and that is exactly the condition that makes the money untouchable and the tax annual at the same time.

The OID rules carry a de minimis escape hatch, and the numbers show why it almost never reaches a bank CD. Publication 550: "You can treat the discount as zero if it is less than one-fourth of 1% (0.0025) of the stated redemption price at maturity multiplied by the number of full years from the date of original issue to maturity." For a five-year CD redeeming at $48,666.11, that threshold is 0.0025 × $48,666.11 × 5, or **$608.33**. The deferred interest is $8,666.11, more than fourteen times it.

## Five years of tax on a balance that has not moved

Take $40,000 in a five-year CD at a hypothetical 4%, compounded annually, with everything payable at maturity. Assume a 22% marginal rate throughout, and set aside state tax.

| Year | Interest accrued | Reported as income | Tax at 22% | Cash available from the CD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $1,600.00 | $1,600.00 | $352.00 | $0 |
| 2 | $1,664.00 | $1,664.00 | $366.08 | $0 |
| 3 | $1,730.56 | $1,730.56 | $380.72 | $0 |
| 4 | $1,799.78 | $1,799.78 | $395.95 | $0 |
| 5 | $1,871.77 | $1,871.77 | $411.79 | $48,666.11 |
| **Total** | **$8,666.11** | **$8,666.11** | **$1,906.54** | — |

The fourth column is the whole problem. By the time the CD matures, **$1,494.75** of tax has already been paid on it — the first four years added together — out of money that came from somewhere other than the CD. The account itself produced no cash at all until the final row.

Now the same $40,000 for five years at a stated 4% paid out monthly, $133.33 a month, nothing compounding inside the account:

| Year | Interest paid out | Reported as income | Tax at 22% | Cash received during the year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $1,600.00 | $1,600.00 | $352.00 | $1,600.00 |
| 2 | $1,600.00 | $1,600.00 | $352.00 | $1,600.00 |
| 3 | $1,600.00 | $1,600.00 | $352.00 | $1,600.00 |
| 4 | $1,600.00 | $1,600.00 | $352.00 | $1,600.00 |
| 5 | $1,600.00 | $1,600.00 | $352.00 | $1,600.00 |
| **Total** | **$8,000.00** | **$8,000.00** | **$1,760.00** | **$8,000.00** |

Both CDs are taxed every year of their term. Only one of them hands over the cash to pay the bill.

| | Compounding, paid at maturity | Paid out monthly |
|---|---|---|
| Interest over five years | $8,666.11 | $8,000.00 |
| Total tax at 22% | $1,906.54 | $1,760.00 |
| After-tax interest | $6,759.57 | $6,240.00 |
| Tax funded from outside the CD | $1,494.75 | $0 |

The compounding CD wins by **$519.57** over five years, about 1.3% of the original deposit, and the price of that win is $1,494.75 of tax paid out of pocket before a dollar can be withdrawn. The gap also understates the payout CD, whose $1,248.00 of after-tax cash each year is available to reinvest. The pre-tax yield difference is the part the rate sheet shows; the cash-flow difference is the part it does not, and reading what a disclosure actually promises is covered in [Six Lines in a Bank Disclosure That Decide What You Earn](/2026/08/24/six-lines-in-a-bank-disclosure-that-decide-what-you-earn/).

## The cash the tax has to come from

Nothing is withheld from a CD by default. A bank takes 24% off the top only when backup withholding has been triggered, which is a name-and-number problem rather than a feature of the account, covered in [Backup Withholding on Savings Interest: Why the Bank Took 24%](/2026/09/21/backup-withholding-on-savings-interest-why-the-bank-took-24/). Absent that, the full accrual is reported and none of it is prepaid. The obligation lands whole, once a year, on a return.

For a $40,000 CD that is a manageable number. Scale it up and the arithmetic changes character. On $250,000 at the same hypothetical 4%, the first year's accrual is $10,000 and the tax at 22% is $2,200, rising each year as the balance compounds — and at higher incomes the net investment income tax sits on top of it. Publication 550 describes that as "a 3.8% tax on the lesser of your net investment income or the amount of your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) that is over a threshold amount based on your filing status," with thresholds of $250,000 for married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse, $125,000 for married filing separately, and $200,000 for single or head of household. A locked CD can push a return over one of those lines using money the taxpayer cannot spend.

Four ways to close the gap, in rough order of cost:

1. **Take the payout option at the counter.** The choice between compounding and monthly payment is usually offered at account opening and is far harder to change afterwards. It costs a slice of yield and removes the funding problem entirely.
2. **Ladder shorter terms.** A rung maturing every twelve months produces cash on a schedule, and the [FDIC national average](https://www.fdic.gov/national-rates-and-rate-caps) rates as of August 17, 2026 make the case on their own: 1.71% at 12 months against 1.36% at 60 months, with every term past a year paying less than the one-year figure. The construction is in [Building a CD Ladder When 12-Month CDs Pay the Most](/2026/08/19/building-a-cd-ladder-when-12-month-cds-pay-the-most/).
3. **Hold the tax money in a liquid account.** Parking each year's estimated tax in a savings account costs the spread between the two rates and nothing else.
4. **Break the CD.** The most expensive option, because the penalty is measured in days of interest and can reach principal. The disclosure rules and the offsetting deduction are in [CD Early Withdrawal Penalties: The Disclosure and the Deduction](/2026/09/22/cd-early-withdrawal-penalties-the-disclosure-and-the-deduction/).

Worth checking before any of these: some deposit agreements permit withdrawal of credited interest without touching principal, which moves the account closer to the payout column. Whether that is allowed, and what it does to the rate on the balance left behind, sits in the account disclosure rather than the rate table. Products built around liquidity rather than yield are compared in [No-Penalty, Bump-Up, and Add-On CDs: When the Variants Pay](/2026/08/28/no-penalty-bump-up-and-add-on-cds-when-the-variants-pay/).

## The one-year line

Everything above turns on a term longer than twelve months. On the other side of that line the treatment reverses, and the reversal is not always an improvement.

Publication 550 handles short accounts in the same paragraph as the deferral rule: "The same is true for accounts that mature in 1 year or less and pay interest in a single payment at maturity" — meaning the interest is income when received or made available, not as it accrues. The OID machinery is switched off for them by an explicit carve-out: "The OID accrual rules generally do not apply to short-term obligations (those with a fixed maturity date of 1 year or less from date of issue)." The list of exceptions to reporting OID as current income repeats it as item 3, "Short-term debt instruments (those with a fixed maturity date of not more than 1 year from the date of issue)."

The reporting follows the same split. The 1099 instructions direct issuers to "report OID on obligations with a term of 1 year or less on Form 1099-INT," so a 12-month CD paying everything at maturity generates one Form 1099-INT in the year it matures and nothing in the year it was opened.

That is simpler, and it concentrates. An 11-month CD opened in March pays all of its interest in one calendar year. A 60-month CD spreads the same total across five returns in roughly equal slices, which is usually the friendlier outcome for anyone near a bracket edge, and the less convenient one for anyone expecting to be in a lower bracket later. The choice of term is a tax-timing decision as much as a rate decision, and the underlying arithmetic of what a rate is worth after tax is worked through in [The Tax Bite on Savings Interest: What Your Real Yield Is](/2026/08/26/the-tax-bite-on-savings-interest-what-your-real-yield-is/).

## Renewal, early redemption, and the accrued amount

Two events end a CD early or start a new one, and both have their own line in Publication 550.

Automatic renewal is not a continuation. "If you renew a CD at maturity, it is treated as a redemption and a purchase of a new certificate. This is true regardless of the terms of renewal." The last sentence forecloses the argument that a rollover the depositor never touched is somehow the same deposit. The old CD is redeemed, with whatever that implies for the accrued interest, and a new instrument begins — new term, new rate, and a fresh OID clock if that term runs past a year. What happens when the institution behind the CD changes hands mid-term is a separate question, covered in [When Your Bank Is Acquired, Not Failed: What Happens to Your CD](/2026/09/03/when-your-bank-is-acquired-not-failed-what-happens-to-your-cd/).

Early redemption creates the mirror image of the annual accrual: income was reported in past years that will never be collected. Publication 550 provides the correction under *Redemption before maturity*: "If, before the maturity date, you redeem a deferred interest account for less than its stated redemption price at maturity, you can deduct OID that you previously included in income but did not receive."

The penalty itself is reported separately. On Form 1099-OID it lands in Box 3, described in the instructions as "interest or principal forfeited because of an early withdrawal of time deposits, such as an early withdrawal from a CD, that is deductible from gross income by the recipient," with the same warning that appears on the 1099-INT version: "Do not reduce the amounts in boxes 1 and 2 by the amount of the forfeiture." Publication 550 points to the same box: "If you forfeited interest or principal on the obligation because of an early withdrawal, the deductible amount will be shown in Form 1099-OID, box 3."

Note what Box 2 of Form 1099-OID is not. It holds "any qualified stated interest paid or credited on this obligation during the year" — actual periodic interest on an instrument that also carries OID. On Form 1099-INT, Box 2 is the early withdrawal penalty. Same box number, two meanings. Whether breaking the CD is worth it at all, before the tax layer, is run in [When Breaking a CD Actually Pays: Run the Break-Even](/2026/08/25/when-breaking-a-cd-actually-pays-run-the-break-even/).

## Frozen deposits, the narrow exception

One situation does leave interest on an unreachable deposit untaxed, and its limits matter precisely because they exclude the ordinary locked CD.

Publication 550: "Exclude from your gross income interest on frozen deposits. A deposit is frozen if, at the end of the year, you cannot withdraw any part of the deposit because:

- The financial institution is, or may become, bankrupt or insolvent, or
- The state in which the institution is located has placed limits on withdrawals because other financial institutions in the state are, or may become, bankrupt or insolvent."

Both triggers involve the institution's condition. Neither is satisfied by a contract the depositor signed. A five-year CD is illiquid by agreement, not frozen by insolvency, and the distinction is the difference between an exclusion and a tax bill.

The measurement rule closes the door further. The amount excluded is the credited interest minus "the net amount you withdrew from these deposits during the year" and "the amount you could have withdrawn at the end of the year (not reduced by any penalty for premature withdrawals of a time deposit)." The parenthesis is decisive: an amount that could have been withdrawn by paying a penalty counts as available, so the penalty does not create a freeze.

A Form 1099-INT that arrives for frozen deposits still goes on the return. Publication 550 sets out the mechanics: include the full amount on Schedule B (Form 1040), Part I, line 1, then "Below this subtotal, enter 'Frozen Deposits' and show the amount of interest that you are excluding. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on Schedule B (Form 1040), Part I, line 2." Receiving that form is itself one of the conditions requiring Schedule B. What happens to a deposit and a CD contract when an institution actually fails is a separate chain of events, set out in [What Happens to Your Money When a Bank Fails](/2026/08/23/what-happens-to-your-money-when-a-bank-fails/).

## Where the numbers land on the return

The destination is ordinary. "Generally, you report all your taxable interest income on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 2b," and OID goes to the same line — Publication 550 says of Form 1099-OID that "In most cases, you must report the entire amount in Form 1099-OID, boxes 1, 2, and 8 as interest income."

Schedule B (Form 1040), Part I becomes mandatory in nine listed situations. Three of them are reachable from an ordinary deposit portfolio: "You had over $1,500 of taxable interest or ordinary dividends," "You received a Form 1099-INT for interest on frozen deposits," and "You are reporting OID in an amount less than the amount shown on Form 1099-OID." The instruction for listing payers is specific about brokered holdings: "If you received a Form 1099-INT or Form 1099-OID from a brokerage firm, list the brokerage firm as the payer."

That third trigger has its own convention. When less OID is reported than the form shows, the difference is displayed rather than silently omitted: "Show OID you do not have to report below a subtotal of the interest and OID listed. Identify the amount as 'OID Adjustment' and subtract it from the subtotal."

The early withdrawal penalty has a fixed destination that does not require itemizing. Publication 550: "You must include in income all interest shown in Form 1099-INT, box 1. You can deduct the penalty on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 18."

A missing form does not remove the obligation. "If you had OID for the year but did not receive a Form 1099-OID, you may have to figure the correct amount of OID to report on your return," with [Publication 1212](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p1212) supplying the method. The $10 daily-portions threshold means small accruals go unreported by the issuer, not untaxed.

## Common questions

**The bank sent a 1099-OID for a CD that has paid me nothing. Is that an error?** Not by itself. The 1099 instructions require the form from "an issuer of a certificate of deposit (CD) made, purchased, or renewed after 1970 if the CD has OID and a term of more than 1 year," and Publication 550 includes OID in income "as it accrues over the term of the debt instrument, whether or not you receive any payments from the issuer."

**Does a penalty on early withdrawal postpone the tax?** Generally no. The constructive receipt rule treats income as received even where the depositor must "Pay a penalty on early withdrawals," and carves out only the case where "the interest you are to receive on an early withdrawal or redemption is substantially less than the interest payable at maturity." A penalty is the norm on time deposits; the exception asks a narrower question, and how it applies to a specific contract is a question for a tax professional.

**Can I deduct interest I reported but never actually collected?** Publication 550 allows it in one defined circumstance: "If, before the maturity date, you redeem a deferred interest account for less than its stated redemption price at maturity, you can deduct OID that you previously included in income but did not receive." The early withdrawal penalty is separate and appears in Box 3 of Form 1099-OID.

**Is a locked CD the same as a frozen deposit for tax purposes?** No. A deposit is frozen only where the institution "is, or may become, bankrupt or insolvent" or a state has limited withdrawals for that reason. The exclusion calculation also counts money that could be withdrawn by paying a penalty as available, "not reduced by any penalty for premature withdrawals of a time deposit."

**Does a shorter CD avoid the problem?** It changes it. Under the short-term carve-out, "The OID accrual rules generally do not apply to short-term obligations (those with a fixed maturity date of 1 year or less from date of issue)," so a 12-month CD paying at maturity reports once, on Form 1099-INT, in the year it pays — no annual accrual, and the entire amount in a single tax year.

The 1099-OID that arrives for a CD with years left to run is not a mistake, and not a preview of a bill that waits for maturity. It is the deferral rule doing what it says, on a deposit whose term crossed twelve months. How much cash that costs was settled at the counter, in the box marked compound or pay out.
